chunks: A digital chip pulls current in sharp bursts, and the regulator is too far away and too slow to supply it, so the capacitors act as tiny local batteries that supply the burst and keep the rail from dipping.
Why so many? A real capacitor isn't just a capacitance.
It has ESR and a small series inductance, so above its self-resonant frequency it stops acting like a capacitor and acts like an inductor.
A big electrolytic might be inductive above a few tens of kilohertz to a megahertz, while a 100 nanofarads 0402 stays capacitive up to roughly 20 megahertz.

The chip's current demand extends to hundreds of megahertz, so you need a mix of values, each covering its own band, and you need lots of small ones in parallel because paralleling divides the inductance.
Why not one massive capacitor? A bigger capacitor has a bigger package, which means more inductance, and it sits farther from the pins, adding more.
So its impedance at 100 megahertz is just 2 pi f L , which is huge. A big cap solves low frequency, but not the high frequency.
Ten 100 nanofarads in parallel have a tenth of the inductance of one, and putting them at the pins keeps the loop small. It also costs less than one very large low-ESL part."
